THE LIVING WORLD — PEOPLE WHO KEEP HAVING TO DEAL WITH THE HEROES

Irreverents • Expansion proposal, not approved canon • 22 November 2026

# The central social premise

This world is steeped in story. People care about heroes, destiny, ceremonies, laws, royal duty and how they will be remembered. They build monuments, record battles and argue over proper meanings. The protagonists care about opportunities to do something extraordinary, with little respect for prescribed significance.

The world must be reactive and emotionally plausible enough that this contrast works even without constant dialogue. NPCs are not props that forget everything as soon as an encounter ends. They are inhabitants capable of gratitude, outrage, fear, admiration, resentment, fascination and dependence simultaneously.

# The wrong abstraction: one morality bar

A town does not switch cleanly from Good Friends to Hostile Criminals. It can be grateful for a rescue, angry about a theft, impressed by the result, afraid of further harm, fascinated by the party, dependent on its power and suspicious of its intentions all at once.

This is an explicit approved direction; the dimensions and numerical representation below are design proposals.

Proposed memory dimensions, tracked per group and (for key NPCs) individually:

Gratitude — perceived help received.

Grievance — harm, betrayal, humiliation, property loss.

Awe — extraordinary capability demonstrated.

Fear — concern over what the party might do next.

Trust — whether the party can be relied on with sensitive access.

Dependence — need for help against forces locals cannot face.

Current heat — immediate security response to active incidents.

These values are not moral judgments. They inform concrete behavior. A person can have high gratitude, high grievance and high awe without contradiction.

# A town's memory example: dragon, cloak, jewels, arena

State 1: dragon threatens town. Locals are anxious; help is welcome.

State 2: heroes save town. Gratitude and awe surge; they receive an invisibility cloak and access to celebrations.

State 3: heroes use cloak to rob the town's prized jewels. Grievance rises, trust collapses; locals are stunned at the betrayal, but still know the heroes saved them.

State 4: townspeople pursue thieves into sealed arena. The trapped crowd becomes terrified; undead gladiators awaken.

State 5: heroes rally with townspeople to fight the dead. Gratitude, dependence and awe return, even while the jewel grievance remains.

State 6: after the incident, different NPCs remember different aspects. One shopkeeper refuses service, another offers a discount, a guard mobilizes faster, a child cheers, an old champion asks to join the roster.

This is the user's illustrative scenario, developed as a social-system example; it is NOT a required quest, character or story chain. The point is simultaneously enduring, conflicting memories.

# Proposed factions and what they value

THE ROYAL COURT: legitimacy, prophecy, ceremony and administrative continuity. Their king is desperately trying to complete a world-saving briefing. Their gratitude for powerful rescuers coexists with fury at public humiliation and treasury theft.

THE CITY WATCH: visible peace, predictable patrols, jurisdiction and safety. They act first on immediate events, not an omniscient judgment of character. Over time, they adapt to known tricks (e.g., guarding vents after repeated thefts).

THE MERCHANTS' COMPACT: secure trade and profit. May bankroll a dragon-slayer banquet, hire investigators after a heist, or reward the very heroes who saved their caravans. Their members disagree.

THE HALL ARCHIVISTS: preserve extraordinary moments, not certify moral goodness. They value credible evidence, unusual deeds and historical context. They react with professional outrage when their institution is attacked but may be compelled to record that outrage as a new legend.

THE KEEPERS OF THE SEALS: sincerely believe the overarching threat could destroy the world. Their frustration at the protagonists grows as they see monumental effort wasted on minor curiosities. Their sources, rituals and motives are provisional.

THE UNDERWAY RESIDENTS: overlooked craftspeople, tunnel inhabitants and secretive creatures who experience the world from below. Outsiders may see them as mysterious; they simply have their own practical concerns and trade in paths rather than public glory.

THE CINDERWORKS ENGINEERS: pride themselves on machines. Their response to grand theft is not only righteous fury but fascination that someone hijacked a supposedly impossible suppression vehicle.

THE ARENA TRADITIONALISTS: cherish honorable combat, wrestling records and public triumph. They may adore a legendary last stand while despising an opportunistic heist.

None of these factions has been approved as canon. Think of them as test cases for different response psychologies.

# NPC archetypes to write and animate

The Believer: reveres the main quest and treats ordinary choices as morally weighty.

The Opportunist: sees how heroic fame creates trade, access and vulnerabilities.

The Rules Keeper: objects more to broken procedure than harm done; excellent comic foil.

The Veteran: recognizes great physical feats and tries to test the party.

The Frightened Ordinary Person: cares about survival, family and a nearby home.

The Curious Child: fascinated by the improbable stunts adults fear.

The Investigator: follows evidence and patterns across regions rather than magically knowing guilt.

The Archivist: records contradictory stories in the same solemn tone.

The Creature: communicates through movement, habits, territoriality or other species-specific patterns; not every creature is a mindless enemy.

The Opportunistic Guard: might retreat, call backup or choose not to fight depending on risk.

# Social interactions without a morality lecture

A hero saves a bakery from a monster; the baker offers pies. The same hero later hurls a guard through the bakery wall. The baker is now furious, still grateful and perhaps begrudgingly impressed. The baker can refuse pie sales, call for help or later request the party to save a missing apprentice. No popup has to explain “your morality decreased.”

Recognizable social cues matter: faces turn, conversations stop, guards take positions, patrons lock doors, shopkeepers hide valuables, children whisper, musicians stop playing, then restart when the threat passes.

# Local incident memory versus long-term history

Immediate incident: “There's a person carrying the stolen chest!” Witnesses and guard searches react to what they actually know.

Regional memory: “Those are the people who broke the east bridge, but they also defeated the dragon.” Rumors and services change with accumulated experience.

Historical memory: “The Day the Royal Champion Was Suplexed Through the Stained Glass.” The Hall, ballads, newspapers or inscriptions may immortalize extraordinary incidents. Historical records do not erase ordinary grievances.

Game systems may represent these on distinct timelines; details are open.

# A proposed NPC state machine, grounded in observable causes

Routine: follows work, patrol, leisure or creature behavior.

Interest: hears a noise, sees trespass, notices missing valuables or sees someone acting strangely.

Investigate: searches, questions bystanders, approaches an object or summons a local ally.

Alert: confirmed wrongdoing or attack; calls for help, guards equipment, pursues or flees.

Escalate: repeated resistance failure or severe danger draws better forces.

Search/Cool: offender vanishes; search tightens at last known location then disperses based on believable rules.

Aftermath: cleanup, medical care, repair, argument, gossip, new vigilance or unexpected admiration.

Characters don't always travel through every state. A dragon may attack immediately; a timid civilian may flee first; an elite champion may challenge rather than call guards.

# How factions learn without becoming unfair

Adaptation should be visible and local: guards barricade a tunnel after a notable infiltration, merchants install shutters on one shop, a museum hires a new security unit after a previous raid. Don't make every NPC omniscient or every previously clever tactic permanently useless.

Learning may create new opportunities: a barred tunnel means a guard must unlock it sometimes; new heavy patrols bring valuable hijackable machines; a prize placed behind stronger defenses becomes a better heist.

# Reputation-dependent play rather than menu outcomes

Revered hero: welcomed through the front door, invited into festivities, offered gifts.

Known menace: guards are wary, but some opponents actively seek to challenge the party.

Distrusted rescuer: still invited to help during real emergencies, but watched closely.

Notorious infiltrator: valuables are locked down; owners may inadvertently reveal new security routes.

Legendary survivor: a public notice warns patrols not to engage without reinforcements; this creates more exciting resistance.

These are combinable reactions, not mutually exclusive reputations or predetermined alignments.

# The war between versions of the same story

An encounter can be recounted as a salvation by one family, betrayal by another and incredible military victory by a retired guard. The Hall attempts to preserve factual gameplay evidence without settling the moral argument.

Ambient chatter might reference achievements the player doesn't remember caring about. This is where the game world can care about narrative far more than the heroes ever will.

# Writing and animation guidelines

Write NPC dialogue as earnest responses to their lived situation, not as nonstop fourth-wall jokes. The funniest line often belongs to someone trying to restore order while the heroes notice something else.

Use compact pixel sprites with strong expressive states rather than huge illustrative facial performances. In calm rooms, let idle animation and understated sound carry emotion. During escalating pursuits, readable signals outrank environmental ornament.

# Ethical and scope considerations for development

NPC reactions must not require simulating a human life for every background resident. Use a few reusable archetypes, local incident events, faction overlays and authored memory beats for important NPCs.

The exact violence presentation and content rating remain undecided. The world need not approve of player violence in order for it to be fun as fictional play. Do not add a punitive morality system merely to condemn experimentation.

# Acceptance tests

The party can save a town, rob that same town and later fight alongside its inhabitants. Several NPCs react differently; the region remembers both helpful and harmful acts; pursuit eventually cools enough that play resumes.

A merchant who hates the party can still be moved by a new rescue, without prior theft vanishing from memory.

The Hall archives the same event with its participants even if local public opinion about it is bitterly contested.
